Daniel’s core claim hinges on a hidden assumption: that “social” presence is equivalent to a judging, remembering human audience. Social psychology tends to treat social influence more broadly—people adjust their speech not only for reputation management but also for coordination with a listener, even a minimal one. The fact that Alexa “needs to understand” already forces what linguists call audience design: you monitor yourself for clarity, normativity, and machine-parseable phrasing. That is a kind of self-awareness, just not the *evaluative* self-awareness Daniel associates with being watched. This distinction matters, because it reframes the experience less as “non-socializing” and more as interacting with a listener that triggers some social-cognitive machinery while short-circuiting others. The tradition Daniel is circling without naming is the “media equation” / “computers as social actors” line of work, which shows that people routinely apply social scripts to machines even when they know they’re machines ([Reeves & Nass, *The Media Equation*](https://archive.org/details/mediaequationhow00reev)).

The other blind spot is empirical rather than philosophical: Alexa may not *feel* judgment, but the system is embedded in an institutional audience. Voice assistants are often designed and improved through data retention, human review, and logging; even when policies change, the user cannot directly observe what is remembered, by whom, and for how long. So the “will not judge me or remember anything” premise is precisely what the interface is optimized to *suggest*, not what the socio-technical system guarantees. If Daniel’s point is about subjective experience, that’s fine—but then the novelty isn’t “speech without an audience”; it’s “speech under the illusion of no audience,” which is closer to a classic recipe for disinhibition than a wholly new category of talk.

A useful expansion would be to name the kind of freedom Daniel is describing: an “audience without accountability” can feel like confession, journaling, or even rubber-duck debugging—except the “duck” is networked, commercial, and asymmetrically informed. That tension is where the interesting social psychology sits: the device invites candor by withholding cues of evaluation, while still extracting value from the interaction. Daniel’s “novel and wild” experience may be less unprecedented than it appears—more a modern redesign of privacy signals, with real consequences for how people calibrate what they say and to whom.
